stories.headline: Supreme Court Strikes Down Trump's Birthright Citizenship Executive Order in 6-3 Ruling
stories.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 to strike down President Trump's executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship, dealing a significant blow to one of the president's signature immigration priorities. The ruling upholds the longstanding interpretation of the 14th Amendment, which grants citizenship to virtually all persons born on U.S. soil regardless of their parents' immigration status.

The decision has drawn sharp reactions across party lines. Republicans who opposed the ruling argued Congress should pursue legislation targeting "birth tourism," with Rep. Byron Donalds calling it "a terrible decision." Some Democrats, including Rep. Ro Khanna, agreed that regulating immigration before entry is appropriate but argued that stripping citizenship from those born on U.S. soil would be unconstitutional.

Democrats broadly praised the outcome. Rep. Christian Menefee said the court "got it right" and called the 14th Amendment's meaning clear, while Rep. Seth Magaziner argued the Constitution's text is unambiguous and that changing it would require a constitutional amendment rather than an executive order.

The ruling represents one of the most consequential legal defeats for Trump's immigration agenda. Following the decision, ICE launched a surge of enforcement activity, making 10,000 arrests in five days. The White House has not yet announced whether it will pursue legislative alternatives to limit birthright citizenship.

stories.headline: Super Typhoon Bavi Bears Down on Guam with Catastrophic 160 mph Winds, Mass Evacuations Underway
stories.summary:
A super typhoon is bearing down on Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, with the U.S. National Weather Service warning of "catastrophic" damage. Typhoon Bavi is forecast to make landfall early Monday with sustained winds of up to 257 km/h (160 mph) and gusts reaching 207 mph, along with waves potentially reaching 35 feet and significant flooding from torrential rain.

Emergency evacuations are underway across both U.S. Pacific territories, with Guam opening five evacuation centers in schools for a population of approximately 170,000. Civil defense officials reported that at least one evacuation site reached maximum capacity Sunday afternoon. The National Weather Service warned the window for safe evacuation was rapidly closing and that winds "will pose a deadly threat to those venturing outside."

Bavi has been classified a super typhoon by the Joint Typhoon Warning Center, a U.S. Navy unit, which predicts sustained winds of 150 knots upon landfall — the equivalent destructive potential of a Category 4 or 5 hurricane. Destructive conditions are expected to persist for eight to 10 hours before and after the storm's center passes over the islands Monday afternoon.

Scientists note the storm is part of a broader trend: Bavi will be the 11th Category 4 or 5 tropical cyclone to hit U.S. Pacific territory in the past decade, more than in the prior 57 years combined. Researchers attribute the increasing frequency and intensity of such storms to climate change and a strong El Niño pattern currently warming Pacific surface waters.

stories.headline: France Awaits Tuesday Verdict That Will Decide Whether Marine Le Pen Can Run for President
stories.summary:
France is bracing for a pivotal court ruling Tuesday as an appeals court in Paris prepares to deliver its verdict on Marine Le Pen's conviction for misuse of European parliamentary funds — a decision that will determine whether the nationalist frontrunner can compete in next year's presidential election. Le Pen, leader of the National Rally party and the leading candidate in current polls, was originally sentenced in March 2025 to two years of home detention and five years of ineligibility from public office, with the ineligibility portion declared immediately effective.

The appeal court will decide whether to confirm, overturn, or modify that sentence. Le Pen was found to have presided over a scheme in which RN staff in Paris were paid using EU parliamentary funds while posing as assistants in Brussels and Strasbourg. Her lawyers have sought acquittal, while the state advocate has again requested five years of ineligibility — which would definitively bar her from the race.

Legal observers are closely watching the possibility of an intermediate sentence. A shorter ineligibility term of two years, for instance, could theoretically allow her to stand, given the election's timing. If barred, RN's candidate would become 30-year-old Jordan Bardella, who polls suggest would also be competitive but whose youth and inexperience could prove liabilities during a campaign.

Le Pen has characterized her original conviction as a politically motivated attempt to prevent her from reaching the presidency, a claim her supporters have amplified. Critics and legal authorities maintain the case is a straightforward prosecution of documented financial misconduct. The ruling carries implications not only for French domestic politics but for the broader trajectory of European nationalist movements.

stories.headline: Chinese Underground Church Leader Released from Prison, Travels to U.S. After Trump Raised Case with Xi
stories.summary:
Jin Mingri, founder of Beijing's Zion Church and one of China's most prominent underground Christian leaders, has been released from prison and has traveled to Los Angeles, less than two months after President Trump directly raised his case with Chinese President Xi Jinping during a state visit to Beijing in May. Jin's family confirmed his arrival in the United States, calling his release "a miracle" and thanking both Trump and Xi for what they described as direct intervention.

Jin was imprisoned following overnight raids across China in October, in what Christian advocacy groups described as one of the harshest crackdowns on unregistered religious activity in China's modern history. Thirty church leaders were reported detained in that round of arrests. Jin's Zion Church, founded in 2007, had grown to approximately 10,000 members across 40 cities before being officially banned by the Chinese Communist Party in 2018 after it resisted government orders to install surveillance cameras on its Beijing property.

The Chinese foreign ministry has not publicly commented on Jin's release. U.S.-based rights group ChinaAid, which monitors religious persecution in China, confirmed the release while cautioning that "countless" other religious practitioners — including eight members of Zion Church — remain incarcerated. The Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, a Western legislative group, welcomed the news.

The release comes amid ongoing U.S.-China diplomatic engagement but does not signal a broader policy shift, according to observers. Trump also raised the case of pro-democracy Hong Kong media owner Jimmy Lai, sentenced to 20 years in prison, during his Beijing meetings. Lai remains imprisoned. China tightly regulates all religious practice and officially promotes state atheism, requiring worshippers to attend only government-sanctioned churches led by state-approved clergy.
